title: Oracy for the masses, Latin for the elite?
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman responds to a weekend argument on social media about oracy and the UK government's plan to make it a centrepiece of English education reform. He takes aim at an article by Baron Daniel Hannan, who questions the value of knowing facts in an age of generative AI, and notes the irony that Hannan's own school, Marlborough College, teaches a knowledge-rich curriculum including Latin and Greek. Ashman calls this view a depressing instrumentalism that could be used to argue away any school subject, and points to E. D. Hirsch's older case against outsourcing knowledge to technology. He then examines the evidence for oracy, observing that the term is vague, that the Education Endowment Foundation has run only two inconclusive pilots of Voice 21, and that the Toolkit's "plus six months" figure for oral language interventions rests on mostly non-significant studies mushed together. He doubts that assessing speaking and listening will help, recalling the farce of his own GCSE exam. He concludes that talk has a place in classrooms but that Hannan owes his success to the knowledge he was taught.
points: Arguing that AI makes knowledge unnecessary is an instrumentalism that could justify removing any subject, and it ignores that elite schools still teach knowledge-rich curricula such as Latin and Greek.
The term oracy is so vague that it can be bent to mean whatever an advocate wants, which makes policy built on it hard to evaluate.
The Education Endowment Foundation Toolkit's headline gain for oral language interventions comes from pooling very different studies, most of which show no significant effect.
Assessing speaking and listening in an exam setting tends to be brief and artificial, so a policy relying on assessment as its lever risks wasting teacher and student time.
Debate, drama and classroom talk are worthwhile, but the real source of a privileged education is the breadth of knowledge taught.
quotes: This depressing instrumentalism—the assumption that education should be judged only by its immediate uses in everyday life—can be used to argue away anything from the school curriculum.
One of the problems with the term ‘oracy’ is that nobody knows what it means. It must involve speaking, but that’s about it.
It is a good tip and one I should commit to for future podcast recordings, but it is not a curriculum.
Hannan appears to be blissfully unaware of both his own educational privilege and the arguments against his dour instrumentalist vision of education.
The Education Endowment Foundation has run two inconclusive pilot trials of the Voice 21 program, but has never scaled this up to a full randomised controlled trial
Studies of often quite different interventions are mushed together to produce a spurious overall effect size that is then converted into ‘additional months of progress’.
It is impossible to do this in an exam hall and so it was assessed by my English teacher and it was necessarily brief. We all knew it was a farce.

But I cannot help thinking Hannan benefited far more from the mathematics, history, geography, modern languages, sciences, classics and more on offer at an elite English institution—knowledge that he now so foolishly disdains.
